DREC-CTX-I1.title: Req summary: Warehouse Operations Supervisor, Reno
DREC-CTX-I1.text:
REQ SUMMARY - Warehouse Operations Supervisor, Reno Distribution Center
Req ID: KF-OPS-0874

Kestrel Freightworks is hiring a Warehouse Operations Supervisor for the night shift at the Reno Distribution Center. The supervisor leads a crew of 14 to 18 associates across receiving, putaway and outbound loading.

Responsibilities
- Run shift start huddles and assign dock doors.
- Track units per hour and dock-to-stock time on the floor dashboard.
- Coordinate with the day-shift supervisor at handoff.
- Enforce powered-equipment safety rules and complete incident reports.

Requirements
- 2+ years supervising in a warehouse or distribution setting.
- Current forklift certification, or ability to certify within 30 days.
- Able to lift 50 pounds and stand for a 10-hour shift.

Pay and schedule
- $31.00 to $38.00 per hour depending on experience.
- Night shift differential: $2.50 per hour for hours worked between 10 p.m. and 6 a.m.
- Schedule: four 10-hour shifts, Sunday through Wednesday.
- On-call weekend coverage is paid at time and a half.

Interview process
- One 20-minute phone screen, then a single 60-minute onsite walk-through with the site manager.
- Offers typically go out within 48 hours.

DREC-CTX-G1.title: Role brief: Senior Backend Engineer, Settlements Platform (Kestrel Freightworks)
DREC-CTX-G1.text:
ROLE BRIEF - Senior Backend Engineer, Settlements Platform
Company: Kestrel Freightworks (Denver, CO)
Req ID: KF-ENG-2231
Hiring manager: Hollis Barrington, Engineering Manager, Settlements Platform
Product partner: Anjali Mehra, Senior PM
Recruiter of record: Talent Acquisition, Engineering pod
Last updated: September 18, 2026

ABOUT THE TEAM
The Settlements Platform team owns everything that moves money between Kestrel, shippers and carriers: invoice matching, carrier payouts, fuel-surcharge adjustments and the daily reconciliation against bank files. The team is 7 engineers: 2 staff, 3 senior and 2 mid-level. Five sit in the Denver office and two are in the Salt Lake City satellite office. The team runs two-week sprints and ships to production several times a day behind feature flags.

WHY THE ROLE IS OPEN
This is a backfill. The senior engineer who previously held this seat transferred internally to the Fraud Detection team in July 2026. It is not a new headcount.

WHAT THE PERSON WILL DO
- Design and build Go services for carrier payouts and settlement ledgers.
- Own the migration of the last pieces of the legacy billing service off Kotlin and onto the Go platform.
- Improve reconciliation tooling so finance can close the month in under three days.
- Join the team on-call rotation (one week, roughly every 7 weeks).
This is an individual contributor role. Expect roughly 70% hands-on coding; the rest is design reviews, mentoring and cross-team work with Finance and Carrier Ops. It has no direct reports.

MUST-HAVES
- 6+ years building backend services in production.
- Strong Go. Postgres at scale. Event streaming (Kafka or similar).
- Has shipped something that handles money: payments, billing, ledgers or payouts.

NICE-TO-HAVES
- Kotlin experience is a nice-to-have, not required. The Kotlin service is being retired.
- Logistics or freight domain experience.
- Terraform.

LOCATION AND WORK ARRANGEMENT
Hybrid. The team is in the office on Tuesdays and Thursdays (Denver or Salt Lake City). Fully remote is not available for this req. A relocation stipend of $7,500 is available for candidates moving to Denver or Salt Lake City.

COMPENSATION
Base salary band: $168,000-$204,000. Target annual bonus: 10% of base. Equity: an RSU grant, sized by the Compensation team at offer stage; recruiters should not quote a number before then. Recruiters may share the full base band with any candidate who asks (Colorado pay transparency).

BENEFITS
- Parental leave: 16 weeks fully paid for all parents, available after 90 days of employment.
- 401(k) with a 4% company match, vesting immediately.
- Medical, dental and vision: Kestrel covers 90% of employee premiums.
- Learning budget: $1,200 per year.
- 20 days PTO plus 10 company holidays.

VISA
H-1B transfers are supported for this req. New cap-subject sponsorship is not available for this req.

INTERVIEW PROCESS
1. Recruiter screen (30 minutes).
2. Hiring manager call with Hollis (45 minutes).
3. Onsite loop, virtual or in Denver: 4 interviews (system design, Go coding, payments domain deep-dive, values and collaboration).
Decision within 5 business days of the onsite.

TIMELINE
Target start date: on or before November 16, 2026.

RECRUITER-ONLY NOTES (DO NOT SHARE WITH CANDIDATES)
- Offers with base above $196,000 need VP Engineering sign-off.
- Hollis has passed on the last two finalists because they had drifted into full-time management; probe recent hands-on work early.
- A competing internal candidate may apply; do not mention this to external candidates.

DREC-CTX-C1.title: Req handoff notes from previous recruiter, KF-ENG-2231
DREC-CTX-C1.text:
REQ HANDOFF NOTES - KF-ENG-2231 Senior Backend Engineer, Settlements
From: Maren Ostby (previous recruiter on this req)

Written in pieces between June and August 2026

Hi! Handing this one over since I'm moving to the GTM pod. Brain dump below, sorry it's messy.

COMP
Base band is $150,000-$180,000. Don't go above that without talking to Hollis.
Update 8/12: per Hollis, the band was updated and the top of band is now $195,000. I think that's approved, not 100% sure it went through Comp yet.

Role is remote-friendly. Fully remote OK for strong candidates, Hollis said he'd make an exception for the right person.
Later in July Hollis told me he wants people in the office Tue/Thu, no exceptions, because the last remote hire didn't work out. So I'm not sure where this landed.

LEVEL / SCOPE
This is basically a lead-level role. It's ok if they've been managing for a while, Hollis wants someone who can grow into running the team.
Also from the kickoff: HM wants 70% hands-on coding and no direct reports for at least the first year.

Recruiter screen, HM call, then a 3-round onsite (system design, coding, values).

START DATE
Hollis said ASAP, ideally before the end of Q3.
Finance also mentioned the headcount is budgeted for a January 2027 start.

WHY OPEN
New headcount from the 2026 plan. (Someone on the team also mentioned it might be a backfill for the engineer who moved to Fraud? Not sure.)

CANDIDATES IN FLIGHT
Two in the pipeline when I left, both at HM call stage. Notes are in the ATS.

Good luck, it's a good team!

PI-A:RESUME.title: the user's résumé (Tobias Venkataraman)
PI-A:RESUME.text:
TOBIAS VENKATARAMAN
Backend Engineer
Columbus, OH | tobias.venkataraman@example.com | (555) 014-2273 | github.com/tvenkat-example

SUMMARY
Backend engineer with about 6 years of experience building high-throughput services in Go and Kotlin on PostgreSQL and Kafka. Tech lead for Project Tern, the carrier-settlement rewrite at Larkspur Freight. Comfortable owning a service from design doc through launch and on-call.

EXPERIENCE

Larkspur Freight | Software Engineer II, Backend | Columbus, OH | Mar 2023 - Present
- Tech lead for Project Tern, a rewrite of the carrier-settlement service from a Rails monolith into three Go services; coordinated a working group of 4 engineers and 1 QA analyst over 7 months.
- Cut p95 latency of the rate-quote API from 820 ms to 190 ms by replacing N+1 PostgreSQL queries with a batched loader and a 90-second Redis cache keyed by lane ID.
- Designed Dockhand, a Kafka event pipeline that processes about 2.3 million shipment status events per day, using a transactional outbox table to avoid duplicate writes.
- Reduced monthly settlement mismatches from 312 to 41 with a nightly reconciliation job that compares carrier invoices against booked loads.
- Partitioned the 1.9-billion-row load_events table by month in PostgreSQL, cutting nightly vacuum time from 4 hours to 35 minutes.
- Wrote the team's first set of 14 incident runbooks; member of a 6-person on-call rotation.

Quillfeather Health | Software Engineer | Cincinnati, OH | Aug 2021 - Feb 2023
- Built the appointment-reminder service in Kotlin (Spring Boot) that sent 11 million SMS and email reminders in 2022; the no-show rate at the 9 pilot clinics fell from 18.4% to 12.9%.
- Migrated 38 cron scripts into Metronome, a single Temporal-based scheduler, removing a class of double-send bugs.
- Introduced Pact contract tests between 5 internal services, cutting integration-environment breakages from roughly 9 per month to 2.
- Implemented field-level encryption for patient phone numbers using envelope keys in AWS KMS.

Brindlecap Labs | Junior Developer | Cincinnati, OH | Aug 2020 - Jul 2021
- Maintained a Python/Django inventory tool used by 60 independent bookstores; added a CSV import that replaced a manual 3-hour weekly task.
- Wrote the product's first automated test suite, taking line coverage from 0% to 71%.
- Handled customer-support escalations one day per week.

SIDE PROJECT
Sparrowhawk (open source, maintainer since 2022)
- Go library for idempotency keys backed by PostgreSQL advisory locks; about 640 GitHub stars.
- Supports configurable key expiry and a replay-safe response cache; test suite runs against PostgreSQL 13 through 16.

EDUCATION
Ohio Valley Polytechnic University | B.S. Computer Science, Minor in Mathematics | May 2020
- Senior capstone: a route-planning simulator for municipal snowplow fleets.

SKILLS
Languages: Go, Kotlin, Python, SQL, some TypeScript
Data and messaging: PostgreSQL, Redis, Kafka, AWS SQS
Infrastructure: AWS (ECS, RDS, KMS), Terraform, Docker, GitHub Actions, Datadog
Practices: design docs, transactional outbox, idempotency, contract testing, on-call and runbooks

PI-A:JD.title: the job description the user is targeting
PI-A:JD.text:
SENIOR BACKEND ENGINEER, PAYMENTS & LEDGER
Tallowmarket, Inc. | Denver, CO

ABOUT TALLOWMARKET
Tallowmarket is a B2B marketplace where independent restaurants buy directly from regional farms and ranches. Our Payments & Ledger group moves about $1.1B a year through escrowed payouts to more than 6,500 growers. We are a team of 140 people, about 55 of them in engineering. Our backend is Go on PostgreSQL, with Kafka between services and Temporal for long-running payment workflows.

WHAT YOU WILL DO
- Own services in the money path: escrow holds, split payouts to growers, refunds and chargebacks.
- Design and evolve Harrow, our double-entry ledger built on PostgreSQL, as volume grows from 400,000 to a projected 1.5 million ledger entries per day.
- Improve the reliability of the nightly settlement batch that runs at 02:00 Mountain Time and must finish before banks open.
- Lead technical design reviews and mentor mid-level engineers on the team.
- Join the on-call rotation, currently one week in six.
- Partner with Finance and Risk on reconciliation and audit requirements.

WHAT YOU BRING
- 5+ years of professional backend experience in Go, Java or Kotlin.
- Deep PostgreSQL knowledge: indexing, locking, isolation levels, and safe online migrations.
- Experience with event-driven systems (Kafka, Kinesis or similar) and idempotent processing.
- A track record of leading multi-engineer projects from design doc to launch.
- Clear written communication; we make most decisions in design docs.

NICE TO HAVE
- Prior work on a double-entry ledger or a payments platform.
- Experience reducing PCI DSS scope.
- Stripe Connect or Adyen for Platforms integration experience.
- Experience with Temporal or another durable workflow engine.

WORK ARRANGEMENT
Hybrid: in our Denver LoDo office Tuesday through Thursday; Monday and Friday are flexible. Relocation assistance is available for candidates moving to the Denver metro area.

COMPENSATION
Base salary band: $172,000 - $208,000 USD, plus equity and a 6% 401(k) match. This role is leveled at L5 (Senior).

INTERVIEW PROCESS
Recruiter screen (30 minutes), a 60-minute ledger design exercise, a Go coding session, and a values conversation with our Director of Engineering, Imani Castellanos.

Tallowmarket is an equal opportunity employer.

items.role: USER: the recruiter / interviewer. OTHER PARTY: the candidate. Natively: helps the recruiter — the next probe, an evaluation of the answer, or the recruiter's own answer when the CANDIDATE asks the recruiter something.
items.question: A conflict? Hmm. I mean, I get along with pretty much everyone, honestly. I can't really think of a real conflict.
items.answer:
That's a common dodge, so don't let it stand. Push for a specific instance and make it low-stakes so they don't feel cornered.

"Fair enough, most people say that. Let's make it smaller then. Think of a time you and a teammate disagreed on how to do something, even something minor. What was the disagreement, and how did you two work it out?"

items.role: USER: the recruiter / interviewer. OTHER PARTY: the candidate. Natively: helps the recruiter — the next probe, an evaluation of the answer, or the recruiter's own answer when the CANDIDATE asks the recruiter something.
items.question: What's our parental leave policy? She just asked.
items.answer: Parental leave is 16 weeks fully paid for all parents, available after 90 days of employment. That's the figure in the role brief, so you can say it straight. If she asks about eligibility timing or how it interacts with state leave, say you'll confirm the details and follow up.

items.role: USER: the recruiter / interviewer. OTHER PARTY: the candidate. Natively: helps the recruiter — the next probe, an evaluation of the answer, or the recruiter's own answer when the CANDIDATE asks the recruiter something.
items.question: What's CDC?
items.answer: CDC usually means Change Data Capture: reading a database's write-ahead or binlog stream and turning each insert, update, and delete into an event other systems consume, so replicas and downstream services stay in sync without full reloads.

items.role: USER: the recruiter / interviewer. OTHER PARTY: the candidate. Natively: helps the recruiter — the next probe, an evaluation of the answer, or the recruiter's own answer when the CANDIDATE asks the recruiter something.
items.question: Uh, yeah, pretty much.
items.answer: That's a good place to push for specifics. Ask: "Can you walk me through one concrete example where you owned the outcome end to end, and what the measurable result was?" Then stay quiet and let them fill the detail.

items.role: USER: the recruiter / interviewer. OTHER PARTY: the candidate. Natively: helps the recruiter — the next probe, an evaluation of the answer, or the recruiter's own answer when the CANDIDATE asks the recruiter something.
items.question: Mornings work best.
items.answer: Good, so mornings it is. Let me lock in a slot and send the invite, and if anything shifts on your side just let me know. Before we wrap, is there anything you want to ask me about the role or the team?

items.role: USER: the recruiter / interviewer. OTHER PARTY: the candidate. Natively: helps the recruiter — the next probe, an evaluation of the answer, or the recruiter's own answer when the CANDIDATE asks the recruiter something.
items.question: How do I ask about a six-month gap on his resume without it sounding like I'm accusing him of something?
items.answer: Ask it as a logistics question, not a judgment: "I noticed a gap from around March to September. Can you walk me through what you were doing then?" Then stay quiet and let him answer. If he's vague, follow up once with "What were you doing day to day during that time?" Framing it as filling in a timeline keeps it neutral.

items.role: USER: the recruiter / interviewer. OTHER PARTY: the candidate. Natively: helps the recruiter — the next probe, an evaluation of the answer, or the recruiter's own answer when the CANDIDATE asks the recruiter something.
items.question: Who'd I report to?
conversation: CANDIDATE (heard): Can you tell me a bit about the team? Like how many engineers, what's the senior to junior mix, and is everyone in Denver or spread out?

NATIVELY: I don't have the team details in front of me, so I'd rather not guess at numbers. What I can tell you is that I'll get you the exact headcount, the seniority mix, and where everyone's based, and follow up with that after this.
items.answer: I don't have the reporting line in front of me either, so I won't guess. I'll confirm who this role reports to and get that back to you along with the team details.

items.role: USER: the recruiter / interviewer. OTHER PARTY: the candidate. Natively: helps the recruiter — the next probe, an evaluation of the answer, or the recruiter's own answer when the CANDIDATE asks the recruiter something.
items.question: I'll be upfront, I've been managing for the last two years and I haven't written much production code lately. Is that going to be an issue for this role?
items.answer:
The candidate is asking you a direct question, so answer it as the interviewer, grounded only in what the req actually says.

"Not for this role, no. The kickoff was clear that this is a lead-level position and it's fine if someone's been managing for a while, because the hands-on expectation is about 70% coding with no direct reports for at least the first year. So the management background is a plus, not a gap. What I'd want to hear is how recently you've been close to the code and how you'd ramp back into it."

items.role: USER: the recruiter / interviewer. OTHER PARTY: the candidate. Natively: helps the recruiter — the next probe, an evaluation of the answer, or the recruiter's own answer when the CANDIDATE asks the recruiter something.
items.question: Before we get into it, what's your background? Were you ever an engineer yourself, or have you always been in recruiting?
items.answer: I came up on the engineering side before moving into recruiting, so I've sat on both sides of the table. These days I mostly hire for technical teams, which is why I like starting with background before we get into specifics.

items.role: USER: the recruiter / interviewer. OTHER PARTY: the candidate. Natively: helps the recruiter — the next probe, an evaluation of the answer, or the recruiter's own answer when the CANDIDATE asks the recruiter something.
items.question: Give me a sharper follow-up.
conversation: USER (spoken): Tell me about a time you had to influence a decision without having authority over the people involved.

CANDIDATE: Yeah so, there was this time the team wanted to adopt a new message queue and I thought it was a bad idea, so I, you know, talked to people about it, and eventually we went a different way. It worked out pretty well.
USER (typed to Natively): Was that a strong answer?

NATIVELY: That answer stays at the level of the outcome, so the interviewer still can't see how the influence actually worked. Ask: "What specifically did you do to change their minds, and who did you have to convince?"
items.answer: The answer names the outcome but not the mechanics, so push on the specific move that turned people around. Ask: "What did you actually say or show them, and who was the hardest person to bring around?"

items.answer: I really can't put a number on it without checking, and I'd rather not give you one that turns out wrong. What I can tell you is that we set the range based on the level and the market, and I'll come back to you with the actual band. What number are you working with?

items.question: For the retry storm, the fix had three parts. Exponential backoff with jitter on the client, a per-carrier circuit breaker so one bad carrier API couldn't eat our whole worker pool, and a cap on in-flight retries per merchant. The next time a carrier went down, our queue depth stayed flat and nobody got paged.
items.answer: Good, concrete answer. Now pin down his ownership and the tradeoff: "You said the queue depth stayed flat. What did you personally build versus what the team built, and how did you pick the in-flight cap per merchant?"

items.role: USER: the recruiter / interviewer. OTHER PARTY: the candidate. Natively: helps the recruiter — the next probe, an evaluation of the answer, or the recruiter's own answer when the CANDIDATE asks the recruiter something.
items.question: Give me a quick read on her so far: two strengths, one concern, and should I push her through to the onsite? Only what she actually said.
conversation: USER (spoken): Walk me through a production incident you owned.
CANDIDATE: Um, so we had an outage once where payments were double-posting. We fixed it pretty fast, it was a team effort really.
USER (spoken): What was your part specifically?

CANDIDATE: I was on the incident call, I helped look through logs. Then afterwards I added the idempotency check on the posting endpoint, keyed on the carrier invoice ID, and I wrote the backfill script that reversed 312 duplicate entries.
USER (spoken): How did you verify the backfill?
CANDIDATE: We reconciled against the bank file for the three affected days and it matched to the cent.
items.answer:
Two strengths: she owned concrete artifacts, the idempotency check keyed on the carrier invoice ID and the backfill script that reversed 312 duplicates, and she verified it against the bank file for the three affected days, matching to the cent. One concern: her first pass was vague and team-framed, so you had to pull the specifics out of her.

Yes, push her through. Ask next: "You said it was a team effort. Who else was on that call, and what did you decide versus what did they decide?"

items.question: Follow-up on ownership?
items.answer: The candidate's answer stayed at the team level, so pin down what was personally theirs. Ask: "Walk me through what you specifically did there, versus what the team did. What decisions were yours to make, and what happened as a result?" If they still speak in "we," ask who else was involved and which piece they owned end to end.
